newsitem.title: GERMANY: EU oilseeds industry sees profitable new season.
newsitem.headline: EU oilseeds industry sees profitable new season.

text.p: Oilseed processors in Europe believe abundant new crop supply of soybeans, rapeseed and sunflowerseed will keep their crushing plants well employed and profitable in the 1997/98 season.
They expect mill buying-in prices of new crop will fall to reasonable levels while demand for oil and meal products will underpin end user prices.
"We're quite confident about the autumn and winter," said Arnd von Wissel, chairman of major oilseed plant Oelmuehle Hamburg AG, (Oelag) which is controlled by Archer Daniels Midland.
"High supply means high utilisation and that's automatically good for margins."
But Oelag, which along with its European competitors declines to specify margins, plans to slow down in the summer.
"Old crop soybeans are too expensive and margins are too low, there's no incentive to produce at full blast," said the raw materials manager at another major west European plant.
"The only exception will be domestic rapeseed, which will be competitively priced out of the August harvest."
U.S. giants ADM and Cargill Inc are major EU crushers via their shareholdings in local plants, alongside the Cereol group, part of Eridania-Beghin Say SA, and Belgium's Vandemoortele NV.
Together, the four account for an estimated 80 percent of Europe's 30 million tonnes of annual crush capacity, which needs more than 50 percent of imported seed to keep going.

The EU in 1997/98 may produce 13.75 million tonnes of 10 key oilseeds versus 12.73 million in 1996/97, Oil World newsletter said, putting world output at 275.80 million and 256.28 million tonnes respectively in the two seasons.
But while accounting for five percent of world output, the EU is due to represent 13 percent of the global crush of 219.02 million in 1996/97, the publication showed.
This is because it consumes vast amounts of seed and tropical oils in its food industry and needs to import ready-made oilmeals and starch feeds for animal feed.
It is also a potential seller of rapeseed as well as sunflower, rape and soybean oils to the world market.
The industry sources said China and other importers were in line for oil imports under the threat of the El Nino weather phenomenon, which may cause drought damage in many countries.
Meal demand should suffer from falling meat demand in the wake of the mad cow disease crisis and a swine fever outbreak in a number of EU countries, which means pig numbers are down.
The EU's meal sellers also fear competition from domestic feed grain and imported starch feeds such as tapioca.
But global demand for meal from broiler and pig industries should keep export supplies tight.

Raw materials supply will flow into the EU from all major producers -- the U.S. may harvest a record soybean crop, Canada's rape harvest will be high and the Ukraine and Russia will export sunseed in search of hard currency earnings.
The EU, on the other hand, may export some rapeseed to Mexico or Japan ahead of the Canadian harvest, and it may sell 200,000-400,000 tonnes to Poland in late 1997, sources said.

The comfortable EU supply balance could be dramatically changed by a number of factors -- changes in U.S. crop weather, which drives benchmark Chicago futures prices, and politically inspired eastern European seed export taxes.
EU legislators and consumers may also deny entrance to Canadian canola (rapeseed) because it has been subjected to genetic modification.
